glosses: An order to do something.

examples.text: I was given a command to cease shooting.

glosses: The right or authority to order, control or dispose of; the right to be obeyed or to compel obedience.

examples.text: to have command of an army
GAGE, at that time, had command of troops near the lakes; and fearing an attack from the Indians, had called for some new recruits from Massachusetts; but the Assembly judged them not necessary.
It wasn't a decisive operation, and Carthage still had command of Spain.

glosses: power of control, direction or disposal; mastery.

examples.text: he had command of the situation
England has long held command of the sea
a good command of language

The Indians had command of the lands and the waters — command of all their beneficial use, whether kept for hunting, 'and grazing roving herds of stock,' or turned to agriculture and the arts of civilization.

glosses: A position of chief authority; a position involving the right or power to order or control.

examples.text: General Smith was placed in command.

glosses: The act of commanding; exercise or authority of influence.

examples.text: Command cannot be otherwise than savage, for it implies an appeal to force, should force be needful.

glosses: A body or troops, or any naval or military force, under the control of a particular officer; by extension, any object or body in someone's charge.

examples.text: I asked myself what I was to do there, now my boat was lost. As a matter of fact, I had plenty to do in fishing my command out of the river.

glosses: Dominating situation; range or control or oversight; extent of view or outlook.

examples.text: He's got good command tonight.

glosses: A command performance.

examples.text: Atkinson […] had hinted to me that the Duke of Richmond was so delighted with my acting that he should not be surprised if there was a second command.

glosses: To order, give orders; to compel or direct with authority.

examples.text: The soldier was commanded to cease firing.
The king commanded his servant to bring him dinner.

glosses: To have or exercise supreme power, control or authority over, especially military; to have under direction or control.

examples.text: to command an army or a ship
Monmouth commanded the English auxiliaries.
Such aid as I can spare you shall command.

glosses: To require with authority; to demand, order, enjoin.

examples.text: he commanded silence
If thou be the son of God, command that these stones be made bread.

glosses: to dominate through ability, resources, position etc.; to overlook.

examples.text: Bridges commanded by a fortified house. (Motley.)

glosses: To exact, compel or secure by influence; to deserve, claim.

examples.text: A good magistrate commands the respect and affections of the people.

glosses: To hold, to control the use of.

examples.text: The fort commanded the bay.
